evidence.title: Infective Endocarditis in Perceval Sutureless Valves: Incidence, Diagnostic Challenges, and Management: An Expert Opinion Review.
evidence.abstract: Sutureless aortic bioprostheses have become an established alternative for surgical aortic valve replacement, particularly in elderly and high-risk patients. The Perceval (Livanova) valve, the most widely studied sutureless device, offers favorable hemodynamic performance and reduced operative times but introduces specific challenges when prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) occurs. Although the incidence of Perceval PVE is low and comparable to that of conventional bioprostheses, this complication is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis is often complex due to acoustic shadowing on echocardiography, making multimodality imaging with transesophageal echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography, and [18F]-FDG PET/CT essential. Microbiological profiles resemble those of other biological prostheses, but perivalvular extension and early mechanical instability are frequent. Management follows general PVE principles but often requires early surgical intervention because of the valve's reliance on radial fixation. This review summarizes current evidence on epidemiology, microbiology, diagnostic strategies, treatment, and prognosis of endocarditis involving the Perceval valve, and identifies areas for future research.

evidence.title: Transcatheter Paravalvular Leak Closure: A Step-by-Step Guide.
evidence.abstract: Paravalvular leak (PVL) remains a clinically important complication after surgical or transcatheter valve implantation, presenting predominantly with heart failure (HF) and/or high-shear hemolysis. While redo surgery can be definitive, contemporary candidates frequently carry prohibitive operative risk, positioning transcatheter PVL closure as a key therapeutic alternative. However, available outcome data are largely derived from observational series and registries with heterogeneity in PVL mechanisms, prosthesis types, imaging protocols, and endpoint definitions. Standardized frameworks-such as those proposed by the PVL Academic Research Consortium-support harmonized PVL grading and clinically meaningful composite endpoints that integrate imaging/hemodynamic results with patient-centered outcomes. Across datasets, the most consistent determinant of benefit is residual PVL severity: procedural efficacy is most commonly defined as achieving ≤ mild residual regurgitation without prosthetic leaflet interference, device embolization, or major complications. This review provides a step-by-step, phenotype-driven approach to transcatheter PVL closure, emphasizing multimodality imaging (TEE and cardiac CT, with adjunct CMR and PET when appropriate), access and support planning tailored to valve position, and morphology-matched device selection-often requiring modular multi-device strategies for elongated crescentic channels, particularly in hemolysis-predominant presentations. We also synthesize evidence on complications and bailout management, with a focus on preventable high-severity events (leaflet impingement, embolization, stroke/air, vascular injury, tamponade) and standardized pre-release safety checks. Collectively, contemporary practice supports high implant success in experienced programs, with clinical improvement tightly coupled to procedural endpoint quality and careful Heart Team selection.

evidence.title: Cardiovascular CT in Bicuspid Aortic Valve Disease: A State-of-the-Art Narrative Review of Advances, Clinical Integration, and Future Directions.
evidence.abstract: Bicuspid Aortic Valve (BAV) disease is recognized as the most common congenital heart condition and is frequently associated with complex valvular and aortic disorders. Cardiovascular computed tomography (CT) has become essential for diagnosing BAV, planning procedures, and evaluating patients after treatment. This is largely due to CT's high spatial resolution and its ability to perform volume imaging effectively. This review provides an up-to-date overview of the increasing role of cardiovascular CT in the management of bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). It covers various aspects, including BAV morphology, optimal sizing for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), and post-procedural monitoring. We highlight significant innovations, such as supra-annular sizing techniques and artificial intelligence (AI)-guided analysis, that position CT at the nexus of anatomy, function, and targeted treatment. Additionally, we address controversies concerning inconsistencies in sizing algorithms, recent classification challenges, and radiation exposure. Future development areas include AI predictive tools, radiomic phenotyping, and CT-guided precision medicine. This synthesis aims to provide clinicians and researchers with a high-level guide to the clinical integration of cardiovascular CT and its future in the BAV population. This review provides the most current, comprehensive synthesis on the pivotal role of cardiovascular CT in BAV management, offering a roadmap for integrating advanced imaging into clinical practice and guiding future research priorities.

warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.lesson: Do not assume VP shunt problems apply to the eShunt. The eShunt's drainage geometry is fundamentally different (short path, no siphon). Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry. Over-drainage is siphon-driven; without a hydrostatic column, it may not occur.

informational.mechanism: Flow reversal obstruction clearing (R3)
informational.lesson: Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Sutureless aortic bioprostheses have become an established alternative for surgical aortic valve replacement, particularly in elderly and high-risk patients. The Perceval (Livanova) valve, the most widely studied sutureless device, offers favorable hemodynamic performance and reduced operative times but introduces specific challenges when prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) occurs. Although the incidence of Perceval PVE is low and comparable to that of conventional bioprostheses, this complication is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis is often complex due to acoustic shadowing on echocardiography, making multimodality imaging with transesophageal echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography, and [18F]-FDG PET/CT essential. Microbiological profiles resemble those of other biological prostheses, but perivalvular extension and early mechanical instability are frequent. Management follows general PVE principles but often requires early surgical intervention because of the valve's reliance on radial fixation. This review summarizes current evidence on epidemiology, microbiology, diagnostic strategies, treatment, and prognosis of endocarditis involving the Perceval valve, and identifies areas for future research.

custody_records.raw_content: Paravalvular leak (PVL) remains a clinically important complication after surgical or transcatheter valve implantation, presenting predominantly with heart failure (HF) and/or high-shear hemolysis. While redo surgery can be definitive, contemporary candidates frequently carry prohibitive operative risk, positioning transcatheter PVL closure as a key therapeutic alternative. However, available outcome data are largely derived from observational series and registries with heterogeneity in PVL mechanisms, prosthesis types, imaging protocols, and endpoint definitions. Standardized frameworks-such as those proposed by the PVL Academic Research Consortium-support harmonized PVL grading and clinically meaningful composite endpoints that integrate imaging/hemodynamic results with patient-centered outcomes. Across datasets, the most consistent determinant of benefit is residual PVL severity: procedural efficacy is most commonly defined as achieving ≤ mild residual regurgitation without prosthetic leaflet interference, device embolization, or major complications. This review provides a step-by-step, phenotype-driven approach to transcatheter PVL closure, emphasizing multimodality imaging (TEE and cardiac CT, with adjunct CMR and PET when appropriate), access and support planning tailored to valve position, and morphology-matched device selection-often requiring modular multi-device strategies for elongated crescentic channels, particularly in hemolysis-predominant presentations. We also synthesize evidence on complications and bailout management, with a focus on preventable high-severity events (leaflet impingement, embolization, stroke/air, vascular injury, tamponade) and standardized pre-release safety checks. Collectively, contemporary practice supports high implant success in experienced programs, with clinical improvement tightly coupled to procedural endpoint quality and careful Heart Team selection.

custody_records.raw_content: Bicuspid Aortic Valve (BAV) disease is recognized as the most common congenital heart condition and is frequently associated with complex valvular and aortic disorders. Cardiovascular computed tomography (CT) has become essential for diagnosing BAV, planning procedures, and evaluating patients after treatment. This is largely due to CT's high spatial resolution and its ability to perform volume imaging effectively. This review provides an up-to-date overview of the increasing role of cardiovascular CT in the management of bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). It covers various aspects, including BAV morphology, optimal sizing for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), and post-procedural monitoring. We highlight significant innovations, such as supra-annular sizing techniques and artificial intelligence (AI)-guided analysis, that position CT at the nexus of anatomy, function, and targeted treatment. Additionally, we address controversies concerning inconsistencies in sizing algorithms, recent classification challenges, and radiation exposure. Future development areas include AI predictive tools, radiomic phenotyping, and CT-guided precision medicine. This synthesis aims to provide clinicians and researchers with a high-level guide to the clinical integration of cardiovascular CT and its future in the BAV population. This review provides the most current, comprehensive synthesis on the pivotal role of cardiovascular CT in BAV management, offering a roadmap for integrating advanced imaging into clinical practice and guiding future research priorities.
